q: Why compute a baseline before training a model?
options: A model only counts if it beats the simplest sensible guess
why: If predicting the average scores nearly as well as your model, the model adds complexity without value.

q: Why hold out a test set the model never sees during training?
options: To make the training set smaller
To estimate how it performs on new data
why: Scoring on the data it learned from rewards memorising. The held-out set approximates the future.

q: You are predicting next week's revenue. Which feature is leakage?
why: Leakage means using information that would not exist at prediction time. Next week's cost is only known after the fact.

q: Train score 0.98 but test score 0.61. What is the most likely problem?
options: Too little regularisation is impossible here
why: A big gap between train and test means the model memorised noise. Simplify it, add data, or regularise.

q: 95% of records are 'Completed'. A model that always predicts 'Completed' scores 95% accuracy. What does that tell you?
options: Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced classes: compare with that baseline and look at precision and recall
why: On imbalanced data, accuracy hides failure on the rare class you probably care about.

q: A module is marked 'Can't run here'. What does that mean?
options: It needs GPUs, cloud or hardware this app does not have, so study it elsewhere
why: The badges are honest about coverage. 'Built here' means something to run; 'Can't run here' means do it with an outside course or free notebook service.

q: As polynomial degree rises, training error keeps falling. How do you know when it has overfit?
options: Validation error gets worse while training error improves
why: Only held-out data shows whether the model learned the pattern or memorised noise.

q: A learning rate of 40 makes the loss grow every step. What is happening?
options: Each step overshoots the minimum, so the loss diverges
why: Too large a step jumps past the bottom of the valley and lands higher up each time.

q: A miss costs 10 times a false alarm. How does the cheapest threshold compare with when both cost the same?
options: Lower, so more cases are flagged
why: When misses are expensive, accept more false alarms to catch more positives, which means a lower cut-off.

q: A column predicts the target almost perfectly (single-feature AUC 0.99). What is the right first reaction?
options: Ask whether you would have that value at prediction time
why: A near-perfect single feature usually records the outcome or something that happens after it.

q: Why does a model need a test set it never trained on?
options: To measure how well it works on new data, not just the rows it memorised
why: A model scored on its own training rows looks better than it is. Unseen rows show whether it generalises.

q: What should you write down before you train anything?
options: The target, the metric and the pass mark
why: Without a target and a pass mark you cannot say whether a model is good enough or whether a change helped.

q: Why is a handful of rows not enough to train a model?
options: It memorises noise, scores swing widely and it will not generalise
why: With few rows the model fits chance patterns, and a different split can give a very different score.

q: Why change only one thing between experiments?
options: So you know which change caused the difference
why: If three things change together you cannot tell which one helped or hurt.
